thread.subject: Board game organisation and why it should be with origamis only

article.subject: Board game organisation and why it should be with origamis only
article.body:
EDIT : Here's the playlist of the tutorials I've been slowly making.

Thought I'd share how I've been reorganising my board games if that can make people want to do the same for their own games. I am a member of a fantastic group, on Facebook, called Les Ludistes Origamistes. They have their own website that can actually calculate the size of the paper you need for whatever box, divider or card holder you want. Unfortunately everything is in French but nothing you can't figure out. The videos are very straightforward even if you don't speak the language, you just follow what the guy does. I suppose the only words you'll need to know are like largeur (width), longueur (length), épaisseur (thickness), boîte (box), feuille (sheet), taille (size), séparateur/diviseur (divider), cartes (cards) and you should be able to use the website rather easily. Their tutorials are videos you can find on 2 different channels here (Les Ludistes Origamistes) and there (Mémo-règles), but all corresponding videos are on the website too.
I'm actually tempted to make my own videos but strictly in English to share this great knowledge, while obviously still crediting them. I am now origami converted. It makes your boxes beautiful, it eases setup and pack up, and it is really cheap as you'll just need paper/cardstock, scissors, pencils, and a ruler. Also, it looks intimidating at first but once you're in it, you just can't stop. It's addictive.


My very first origamisation was for the board game Nidavellir. I made a box around the coin rack so the coins are always in place and it eases setup by a mile. Also there's boxes with dividers and small corolla boxes as drawers to keep the coins of every player separated. When people are playing, you just take the drawer and give it to them. Great and simple box to make to hold resources (it opens up when you play).


Then I did a full revamp of the Abyss box to welcome all the expansions in the box, as my second organisation. It was a lot of work for the beginner that I was. I actually made a quick video about it as I streamed the whole process on Twitch. It eases setup as well as you just take the boxes out of the cardboard box, open them, and place them on the table. Then when it is done, you just put everything back in the box and it's done!

Legendary Inventors and its original not paper hungry boxes to hold the players' cubes. Also like for a few other board game boxes, I made my own insert with dividers cause the cardboard divider was actually useless.

Probably my biggest pride is the card shoes made for the decks of It's A Wonderful World and Dune : Imperium. These are the combination of a Moda Masu box with 2 Baggi boxes. When in the box, it holds the cards still. When you want to play, you pull the top Baggi box and push the side strips of the Moda Masu. Then you lock the edges with the Baggi box. It makes a tray where it is easy and quick to draw cards while staying still on the table.

One of my most recent works as I received Stardew Valley fairly recently. I also streamed the process and made a video about it. It was a lot of work but totally worth it as the box can actually close now. It used to be impossible because with the two trays and the fish + minerals/artifacts bags, the box would be too full to close properly. Now everything is easy to pull out of the box when you desire to play and it closes properly too.

I obviously won't post all the origamisations I've made but I made a small album on Imgur if that interests anyone. It features other games such as Descent 2nd Edition, Detective Club, Dune : Imperium, Game of Thrones 1st Edition, Human Punishment Social Deduction 2.0, Not Alone, Sagrada with 5-6p expansion, Sushi Go! Party, When I Dream...
My next projects will probably be Dream Runners, Wingspan and Red Rising. Also a quick origamisation of BANG! would be great too (too many cards that go everywhere in the box).


The other not so obvious advantage to convert yourself to origamising your games is that it keeps your cat busy instead of knocking everything off the table. The cat will think you just took a bed out for him and will be delighted! 😁

article.body:
Thank you so much. I actually had a quick look, I am not sure how to post on it with the links to the board games. I am rather new to the forums of BGG.

The basic Masu boxes (the ones that are mainly used in this list) are really easy to make and I definitely started there too! But I prefer to be able to have boxes of specific measurements instead of all boxes to be squares and with a height of half the length of the box so that is why I was tempted to try to share this knowledge with others. 😄 Seems like this community is pretty big among the French board gamers on Facebook, but living in Australia, all my friends are always amazed at my boxes. Seems pretty unknown here and people just buy expensive inserts instead.

For the V pockets, I believe they're actually the first thing I tried with my Nidavellir cards and was like "Wow, it's that easy!" and then, you couldn't stop me. Very handy and pretty looking holders, imo. When you want to take the card, you open the right strip, and when done, you place your cards in and lock it with the right strip under the left one.
The measurement of the strip of paper you need is fairly simple. Here's the video from their channel. You need the width of a card (example in the video 67mm), and the thickness of the deck (12mm) + 1mm. The strip will be as is :
height : width of the card / example in the video = 67mm
length : (4 x width) + (2 x (thickness of the deck + 1mm)) / example in the video = (4 x 67) + (2 x 13)
Then you just follow what he's doing.

article.subject: Re: Board game organisation and why it should be with origamis only
article.body:
I'm not sure which example you're talking about but your pockets look really awesome!

I tweak by 1 or 2mm depending on the thickness of my paper too. I have relatively thick paper. I am not sure what you used but the ones I got have the thickness written on it. For example, this one is 210GSM. I also have metallic paper that is 180GSM. For the record, normal paper for printing or writing is between 80 and 100GSM. So it is definitely thicker and harder to fold, also adds thickness in the folds which makes me tweak it a little bit just in case.

Also, when you make a V pocket, it gets longer the wider your cards are. The thickness of the deck is minimal (I mean unless you have a really thick deck of cards but in this case I do not believe the pockets are the most optimal solution). I sometimes don't have enough paper so I stick papers together and hide the ugly bits in either the left or right triangular flappy sides. You can see that on my most recent pocket. The cards were 124mm wide which is massive so I needed a band of paper of 51.5cm lol

Iirc I think I put a green band of paper of 124x300mm with a pink one of 124x215mm and hid the tape in the left flappy thingy.

article.subject: Re: Board game organisation and why it should be with origamis only
article.body:
Man I'm so glad you're enjoying it. I do think it is very relaxing too. Hopefully you can find great cardstock! Lots of choices, patterns and sizes! 😄
I think 300x300 is usual where I am but could depend on stores and even countries. But yes, you can do just like me. I tend to stick papers together a lot because I am a maniac and I hate wasting paper so I just reuse old scrap paper from older projects. I also do it with boxes sometimes (but a bit harder cause of the many folds you gotta do) as you never see the back of the paper, I hide the ugly bits inside.

The MM boxes are also quite straightforward. I think it is important to not start too complicated and overwhelm yourself anyway 🙂

The calculation for the required paper is as followed :
Paper size = (Length + Width + 4 x Height) ÷ √2
So for example, I want a box of 50 x 70 x 20mm, my required paper would be (70 + 50 + 4 x 20) ÷ √2 = 141.42mm
But on the website, it calculates everything for you so that's 100x more convenient. Then, you trace the diagonals on your square. From the centre, on diagonal 1, you mark symmetrically half length and twice the height (so it should look like height, height, half length, centre point, half length, height, height). Then, on diagonal 2, you do the same with the width so like height, height, half width, centre, half width, height, height. Once this is all done, you should see that your box dimensions are the rectangle in the centre of your page.
Start folding all the markings. I use a sculpting tool I use in polymer clay but you can use anything to point on a marking then pull the corner of the paper and align it with its diagonals.
Then there's two techniques, the most common one is to mark diagonals for folding but in the group, they actually cut the paper so there's less thickness in the height of the box and the edges are a bit sharper. You can follow what the guy does here. "Le pliage traditionnel" at 5:33 is the traditional way to do it (he also shows how he does his markings. Then the part where he shows how to make a lid at 14:47, he uses the other technique where we cut the borders of the box (the one I use for all my boxes cause my paper is very thick).

I actually just buy regular cardstock from Kmart Australia. Some fancier ones from Spotlight (but they're super expensive). I actually love the cheap ones from Kmart because eventhough they don't have patterns (just colours), they are really thick and they make really sturdy boxes or pockets.
When you buy cardstock, you should look for the thickness of the paper, it is usually mentioned. Most of my cardstock paper is usually 210GSM and regular printing paper is usually about 80GSM. I found that actual origami paper is too thin and flimsy but they obviously do work too. I just like them less to work with, it is obviously a preference.
Also I usually try to find cardstock that is 30x30cm cause most boxes require between 20 to 30cm and seeing I mostly make MM, the sheet must be a square so I tend to avoid A4. I sometimes glue or tape sheets together and hide it all on the inside though.

Your pockets look really great and if you're saying they work, that's also what matters the most!
I personally love simplicity and plain white is lovely. Hopefully you get to find the kind of paper you like though if you prefer thicker ones.

And thank you for the compliments! My first video has finally been added to the official channel so I'm super happy. I am actually aiming to make more streams when I have time on my own channel (No Wonders) so I take time origamising board games but it is really so time consuming hence why my last stream and sped video were 2 weeks ago.
I really want to do Wingspan, as well as lots of small board game boxes that definitely need some kind of dividers inside the box as well as pockets like Oriflamme (somehow my favourite game ever didn't even get reorganised and everything is dumped in this small box lol).

article.subject: Re: Board game organisation and why it should be with origamis only
article.body:
I remember I looked at all my scrap papers, tried to find the same thickness for all then assembled all of them on the table on the "back" side up (there's a "paper flat" side and a textured side) and I taped all the pieces together. Then when that was done, I trimmed the whole piece as a square for the correct measurements of the box and got to the folding part.
Normally, for that part, you don't need any glue whatsoever but I like to put some at the bottom to make it look really flat so I would assume I did put a bit of glue yeah lol

I've done that with a bunch of projects where you require too much paper or a piece of paper way too big. The biggest downside is when the fold is on or close to one of the taped pieces because it might lift a bit when you fold which isn't super aesthetically pleasing. That Ark Nova box doesn't have that problem as the parts were the different papers connect are right in the middle of the box and not on the folds.

And thank you for the tutorials 🙂 I just learned of them last week, and just yesterday made my first test v-pocket for a prototype game I saw submitted to a contest:

I hope to continue testing the container designs, and hopefully try and calm down somewhat my struggle with the infamously messy Game: Shadows of Brimstone

article.subject: Re: Board game organisation and why it should be with origamis only
article.body:
Oh, Game: Shadows of Brimstone is a lovable sprawling mess, there's no containing it 😂


There's a saying in the community, that SoB organization is a game of its own. And the ritualized answer to a traditional rite-of-passage question asked by a newbie, "How do I store this game?", is: "You need to buy a bigger house" 😜
An example of someone's storage solution, from when the game had still much less content available than today:

Here's one vid on the topic by The Dungeon Dive, if you're reckless enough to dare tipping your toe into the rabbit hole (be careful to not let it suck you in!): Shadows of Brimstone - Part 23 - Let's Store This SOB!
Fortunately, the game is not for everyone, it's widely dismissed as old-school ameritrash with no interesting mechanics, which it generally is! Thus, many people need not to be much afraid they might like it. The one thing it has for itself, and where it's king, is theme. And a particular, non-mainstream one. So, the warning is directed mostly at anyone who's strongly into [microbadge=51064] and/or [microbadge=55646], and fine with deep [microbadge=35268].
But I don't want to derail this thread, so I'll stop here 😅
